subject: Computer Networking
title: POP3 — Downloading Mail
description: A micro-lesson that makes POP3 — Downloading Mail usable.

hook.text: Before IMAP, there was POP3. Download your mail, delete it from the server. Simple and offline.

buildup.text: POP3 connects to the server, downloads all new messages, and optionally deletes the server copies.

discovery.text: Once downloaded, emails live only on your device. No sync, no multi-device access by default.

twist.text: POP3 is still useful: low-bandwidth areas, archival setups, or privacy-focused users who want local-only storage.

climax.text: Some clients keep copies on the server with 'leave on server.' A workaround, but not true sync.

punchline.text: POP3 downloads and deletes. Simple, but not synced.

quiz.question: What happens by default after POP3 downloads email?
options: The email is marked as read on all devices
A backup is sent to a second server

details.summary: Post Office Protocol version 3 downloads email from a server to a local device, typically deleting the server copy. Designed for single-device access, POP3 is simpler than IMAP but does not sync between devices. It remains useful for bandwidth-limited connections and local archiving.
details.whyItMatters: POP3 was the original way people accessed email remotely. Understanding it explains why some users lose email when switching devices and why IMAP became necessary.
takeaways: POP3 downloads email to the device and removes server copies
It works best when accessing email from a single device
POP3 is simpler than IMAP but lacks synchronization

faq.question: When is POP3 still a good choice over IMAP?
faq.answer: POP3 works well when server storage is limited, bandwidth is constrained, or you want local offline access to all email. It is also useful for archiving: download all mail locally and free server space. But for multi-device access, IMAP is clearly superior.

faq.question: Can POP3 be configured to leave mail on the server?
faq.answer: Yes. Most POP3 clients can be set to leave a copy on the server. However, this does not provide true synchronization. Read status, folder organization, and flags are not synced. It is a workaround, not a replacement for IMAP's full sync capabilities.
